title: Probability: Events, Conditioning and Bayes' Rule
description: Sample spaces and the axioms of probability, counting, conditional probability, independence and Bayes' rule.
overview: Machine learning deals in uncertainty: noisy measurements, finite samples, unobserved causes and unpredictable futures. Probability is the language for it. A classifier outputs the probability of a class, a loss function is the negative log of a probability, and learning is the updating of beliefs in light of data. Every later method in the Machine Learning book is built on the ideas here.

This chapter develops the rules: what a probability is, how to count outcomes, how probabilities change when we learn something (conditioning), when events are independent, and how to reason backward from effects to causes with Bayes' rule.
objectives: State the axioms of probability and derive the rules for complements and unions.
Count outcomes with permutations and combinations.
Compute conditional probabilities, use the chain rule and the law of total probability, and test independence.
Apply Bayes' rule to diagnostic problems, and explain the base rate fallacy.

sections.title: Sample spaces, events and the axioms
body: A random experiment has a set of possible **outcomes**, the **sample space** Ω. An **event** is a subset of Ω, a collection of outcomes. For a roll of two dice, Ω has 36 outcomes (a, b), and 'the sum is 7' is the event {(1, 6), (2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 3), (5, 2), (6, 1)}.
A **probability measure** P assigns each event a number so that (Kolmogorov's axioms):

list: If events A₁, A₂, … are **mutually exclusive** (no two can occur together), then P(A₁ ∪ A₂ ∪ …) = P(A₁) + P(A₂) + ….

body: Everything else follows. The **complement** rule: P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A). The monotonicity rule: if A ⊆ B then P(A) ≤ P(B). And for any two events,

body.eq: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)

body: which is **inclusion–exclusion**: adding P(A) and P(B) counts the overlap twice, so subtract it once.

body: When the outcomes are equally likely, P(A) = |A|/|Ω|, and probability becomes counting.

example.title: Two dice
example.problem: Roll two fair dice. Find P(sum = 7) and P(at least one six).
example.solution: There are 36 equally likely outcomes. Six give a sum of 7, so P = 6/36 = 1/6. For 'at least one six' use the complement: no six has 5 × 5 = 25 outcomes, so P = 1 − 25/36 = 11/36. By inclusion–exclusion: 1/6 + 1/6 − 1/36 = 11/36 ✓.

sections.title: Counting
body: With equally likely outcomes, probability reduces to counting.

list: **Multiplication rule**: if one choice can be made in a ways and then another in b ways, the pair can be made in ab ways.
**Permutations**: the number of orderings of n distinct objects is n! = n(n − 1)⋯1. The number of ordered selections of k from n is n!/(n − k)!.
**Combinations**: the number of unordered subsets of size k from n is the **binomial coefficient** C(n, k) = n!/(k!(n − k)!). Dividing by k! removes the ordering.
**Multinomial coefficient**: the ways to split n objects into groups of sizes k₁, …, k_m is n!/(k₁!⋯k_m!).

example.title: Poker hands
example.problem: How many 5-card hands are there from a 52-card deck, and what is the probability of being dealt four aces?
example.solution: C(52, 5) = 2,598,960. Four aces plus any one of the 48 other cards: 48 hands. P = 48/2,598,960 = 1.85 × 10⁻⁵.

example.title: The birthday problem
example.problem: In a group of 23 people, what is the probability that two share a birthday (365 equally likely days)?
example.solution: Use the complement. The probability that all 23 birthdays differ is (365/365)(364/365)⋯(343/365) = Π_{k=0}^{22}(1 − k/365) ≈ 0.4927. So P(shared) ≈ 0.507, a little over one half. The number of pairs, C(23, 2) = 253, is large: that is why the result seems surprising. The same collision effect governs hashing and the 'birthday attack' on short hashes.

body: Counting appears throughout machine learning: the number of Boolean functions on n bits is 2^{2ⁿ}, the number of ways to choose k features from n is C(n, k), and the number of polynomial features is a binomial coefficient (see Linear Regression). The binomial coefficients also give the coefficients of (a + b)ⁿ = Σ C(n, k)a^k bⁿ⁻ᵏ.

sections.title: Conditional probability and independence
body: The **conditional probability** of A given that B has occurred is

body.eq: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B),    P(B) > 0

body: Learning that B happened shrinks the sample space to B; P(A | B) is the share of B in which A also occurs. Rearranging gives the **multiplication rule** P(A ∩ B) = P(B)P(A | B), and for several events the **chain rule**:

body.eq: P(A₁ ∩ A₂ ∩ … ∩ A_n) = P(A₁) P(A₂ | A₁) P(A₃ | A₁ ∩ A₂) ⋯ P(A_n | A₁ ∩ … ∩ A_{n−1})

body: This is the factorization that underlies autoregressive language models and Bayesian networks.

It computes the probability of an event by averaging over the possible cases. Sums in a mixture model, a Markov chain step and the marginal of a joint distribution all use it.

Events A and B are **independent** if learning one tells nothing about the other: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B), equivalently P(A | B) = P(A). Independence is a modeling assumption that makes joint probabilities multiply, and it is behind the 'i.i.d.' assumption in learning.

body.warn: Independence is not the same as being mutually exclusive. If A and B are mutually exclusive and both have positive probability, they are strongly //dependent//: knowing that A occurred tells us that B did not. Three events can be pairwise independent without being mutually independent.

example.title: Checking independence
example.problem: Roll one fair die. A = {even}, B = {1, 2, 3, 4}. Are A and B independent?
example.solution: P(A) = 1/2, P(B) = 2/3, and A ∩ B = {2, 4} has probability 1/3 = (1/2)(2/3). They are independent.

body: Two events are **conditionally independent** given C if P(A ∩ B | C) = P(A | C)P(B | C). Independence and conditional independence are unrelated in general: two symptoms may be dependent overall but independent given the disease, which is the naive Bayes assumption.

sections.title: Bayes' rule
body: Conditioning is not symmetric: P(A | B) ≠ P(B | A) in general. **Bayes' rule** converts one into the other. From P(A ∩ B) = P(A | B)P(B) = P(B | A)P(A),

body.eq: P(H | E) = P(E | H) P(H) / P(E),    P(E) = Σ_j P(E | H_j) P(H_j)

body: For a hypothesis H and evidence E, P(H) is the **prior** (belief before the evidence), P(E | H) is the **likelihood**, P(E) normalizes by the law of total probability, and P(H | E) is the **posterior**. This is the whole logic of Bayesian learning: update beliefs about parameters or classes after seeing data.

example.title: A diagnostic test
example.problem: A disease has prevalence 1%. A test is positive for 90% of the sick and for 5% of the healthy. A patient tests positive. What is the probability of disease?
solution: Only 15%. The healthy group is so much larger that its 5% false positives (0.0495 of the population) outnumber the true positives (0.009) five to one. Neglecting the prior, the **base rate fallacy**, leads people to answer 90%.

body: Dividing Bayes' rule for H by the same rule for Hᶜ gives the odds form:

body.eq: P(H | E)/P(Hᶜ | E) = [ P(H)/P(Hᶜ) ] × [ P(E | H)/P(E | Hᶜ) ]

body: posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio. Independent pieces of evidence multiply their likelihood ratios, so a second positive test of the same quality in the example (likelihood ratio 0.9/0.05 = 18) turns the odds 0.154/0.846 = 0.182 into 0.182 × 18 = 3.27, a probability of 0.766. Today's posterior is tomorrow's prior.

example.title: The Monty Hall problem
example.problem: You pick door 1 of three, behind one of which is a car. The host, who knows where the car is, opens door 3 to reveal a goat. Should you switch to door 2?
example.solution: Let C_i be 'car behind door i' (prior 1/3 each) and H₃ be 'host opens door 3'. P(H₃ | C₁) = 1/2 (host chooses between 2 and 3), P(H₃ | C₂) = 1 (host must open 3), P(H₃ | C₃) = 0. By Bayes' rule, P(C₂ | H₃) = (1/3)(1)/[(1/3)(1/2) + (1/3)(1) + 0] = (1/3)/(1/2) = 2/3. Switching wins with probability 2/3. The host's choice carries information because it depends on where the car is.

body: Bayes' rule applied to a classifier gives the generative classifier P(y | x) ∝ P(x | y)P(y) (see Generative Classifiers), and applied to model parameters gives the posterior of the Bayesian methods chapter.

summary: A probability measure on a sample space satisfies P ≥ 0, P(Ω) = 1 and additivity for mutually exclusive events. P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A) and P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).
With equally likely outcomes, count: n! orderings, C(n, k) = n!/(k!(n − k)!) subsets.

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). The chain rule factors a joint probability; the law of total probability averages over a partition. Independent events satisfy P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B), which is different from being mutually exclusive.
Bayes' rule: P(H | E) = P(E | H)P(H)/P(E); in odds form, posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio. Ignoring the prior is the base rate fallacy.
These rules underlie generative classifiers, graphical models and Bayesian learning.

problems.q: A box has 5 red and 3 blue balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. Find the probability that both are red, and that the second is red.
problems.solution: Both red: (5/8)(4/7) = 20/56 = 5/14. Second red, by total probability: (5/8)(4/7) + (3/8)(5/7) = 20/56 + 15/56 = 35/56 = 5/8, the same as the probability that the first is red.

problems.q: A factory has three machines producing 50%, 30% and 20% of the output, with defect rates 1%, 2% and 5%. A random item is defective. What is the probability it came from machine 3?
A spam filter flags 95% of spam and 2% of legitimate email. 30% of all email is spam. What fraction of flagged emails are spam?
How many different 4-letter 'words' can be formed using the letters of MATH (each once), and how many 3-element subsets does a 7-element set have?
Events A and B satisfy P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A | B) = 0.8. Find P(A ∩ B), P(B | A) and say whether they are independent.
problems.solution: P(A ∩ B) = P(A | B)P(B) = 0.4. P(B | A) = 0.4/0.6 = 0.667. Since P(A | B) = 0.8 ≠ P(A) = 0.6, they are not independent.
